title: Sarah Schenirer
hookLine: a Kraków seamstress who founded the Bais Yaakov girls' schools in 1917

cards: A sewing room in Kraków, in Poland. Fabric on the table, pins in a cushion, a woman measuring a customer for a dress. Her name is Sarah Schenirer, and she is a seamstress.

As she works, she listens. The girls and young women who come to her for clothes talk about novels, theater, new ideas from the wider world. Some of them, she notices, know very little of their own tradition.
Their brothers spend their days learning Torah; the girls have nowhere to go for it. In 1917, with no money, no title and no school building, she does something about it.

teach.h: A SMALL CLASS IN HER OWN ROOMS.
teach.b: She began with a small class of girls in her own rooms, and called the school Bais Yaakov, the house of Jacob. The name comes from a verse.
At Mount Sinai, just before the Ten Commandments, God tells Moses: "Thus shalt thou say to the house of Jacob, and tell the children of Israel." Why say it twice?

teach.h: THE HOUSE OF JACOB MEANS THE WOMEN.
teach.b: An old rabbinic reading answers: the house of Jacob means the women, and the children of Israel the men. In that reading, the women were addressed first, and she made it her school's name.
This was not a protest against her community. She was a devout woman in a traditional world, and she went looking for the support of respected rabbis, and found it. Her argument was simple.
Girls would be the mothers and teachers of the next generation, in a world full of every other idea, so they needed to know their own texts, prayers and history, seriously. So she taught them.
Then she trained young women as teachers and sent them out to start more schools.
Her one room grew into a movement of schools across Poland and beyond. Bais Yaakov schools still exist today in many cities, teaching what she wanted taught: that girls belong in Jewish learning.
A seamstress makes a garment one measurement, one cut, one seam at a time. She built a school system the same way.

how: Bais Yaakov schools today teach girls Torah, prayer, Jewish law and history, largely within Orthodox and Haredi communities, and they trace their story back to Sarah Schenirer's first class in Kraków.

games.q: you're a seamstress in Kraków. the girls you sew for know little of their own tradition, and there's no school for them. what do you do?

practice: Picture a girl you know, a daughter, a niece, a student, a neighbor's kid, or a girl somewhere you'll never meet. Think about what she's learning right now, and who is helping her learn it.
Hold her there for a while, with the hope that someone answers her questions properly instead of quickly.
